lessons.title: Hello Go: modules and go run
lessons.body:
## Setup

A Go project starts with a **module**: `go mod init example.com/app` creates `go.mod`. Source lives in packages; `package main` with a `main()` func is an executable.

## Run and build

`go run .` compiles and runs in one step. `go build` produces a single static binary — no runtime needed on the target.

## Formatting

`gofmt` (or `go fmt`) is non-negotiable: one canonical style, zero debates.

codeSamples.title: First program

lessons.title: Variables, types, and zero values
lessons.body:
## Declarations

`var x int = 3`, or short form `x := 3` inside functions. Go is statically typed with inference.

## Zero values

Every type has a zero value: `0`, `""`, `false`, `nil`. There is no uninitialized memory — declared variables are always usable.

## Constants and iota

`const` values are compile-time. `iota` auto-increments for enum-like sets.

codeSamples.title: Short vars and iota
codeSamples.code:
name := "Corgi"
count := 0

const (
  Red = iota // 0
  Green      // 1
  Blue       // 2
)

lessons.title: Control flow: if, for, switch
lessons.body:
## One loop to rule them all

Go has only `for` — it covers `while`, infinite loops, and classic counting loops.

## if with init

`if v, err := f(); err != nil { ... }` scopes the variable to the branch.

## switch

No fallthrough by default; cases can be expressions or types. `switch` with no condition replaces long `if/else` chains.

codeSamples.title: for variants

lessons.title: Functions, multiple returns, defer
lessons.body:
## Multiple returns

Go functions commonly return `(value, error)`. This convention drives the whole error-handling model.

## Named returns and defer

`defer` schedules a call to run when the function returns — perfect for cleanup (closing files, unlocking). Deferred calls run LIFO.

## First-class functions

Functions are values: pass them, return them, store them in structs. Closures capture surrounding variables.

codeSamples.title: Return + defer

lessons.title: Strings, runes, and bytes
lessons.body:
## UTF-8 by default

A Go `string` is an immutable sequence of **bytes**, usually UTF-8. Indexing gives a byte; ranging gives **runes** (Unicode code points).

## Building strings

Use `strings.Builder` in loops to avoid quadratic concatenation. The `strings` package has all the helpers (`Split`, `Contains`, `TrimSpace`).

## Conversion

`[]byte(s)` and `[]rune(s)` convert; `string(b)` converts back.

codeSamples.title: Builder + range

lessons.title: Slices: len, cap, and append
lessons.body:
## Slice vs array

Arrays have fixed size; **slices** are dynamic views over a backing array with `len` and `cap`. Most code uses slices.

## append

`append` may allocate a new backing array when capacity is exceeded — always reassign: `s = append(s, x)`.

## Gotcha

Slices sharing a backing array can alias each other. `copy` or a full slice expression avoids surprising mutations.

codeSamples.title: Grow a slice

lessons.title: Maps and the comma-ok idiom
lessons.body:
## Basics

`make(map[K]V)` creates a map. Reading a missing key returns the zero value — use the **comma-ok** form to distinguish absent from zero.

## Iteration order

Map iteration order is **randomized** on purpose; never rely on it. Sort keys if you need order.

## Nil maps

Reading a nil map is fine; writing panics. Always initialize before writing.

codeSamples.title: comma-ok

lessons.title: Structs, methods, and embedding
lessons.body:
## Structs

Go's data type is the `struct`. Attach behavior via **methods** with a receiver. Use a pointer receiver to mutate or avoid copying large structs.

## Embedding

Go favors **composition**: embed a struct to promote its fields/methods — no inheritance, but similar reuse.

## Constructors

Go has no constructors; use a `New...` function returning the value or pointer.

codeSamples.title: Method + pointer receiver

lessons.title: Pointers and value semantics
lessons.body:
## No pointer arithmetic

`&x` takes an address, `*p` dereferences. Go pointers are safe — no arithmetic, no dangling (the GC keeps referenced memory alive).

## When to use pointers

- Mutate the caller's value.
- Avoid copying large structs.
- Signal optional/absent with `nil`.

## Value semantics

Structs are copied on assignment and function calls. Small value types are cheap and cache-friendly — don't reach for pointers reflexively.

codeSamples.title: Mutate via pointer
codeSamples.code:
func double(n *int) { *n *= 2 }

x := 21
double(&x)
fmt.Println(x) // 42

lessons.title: Errors: wrapping and sentinels
lessons.body:
## error is a value

Errors are ordinary values implementing `error`. Check and return them explicitly — no exceptions.

## Wrapping

Add context with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)`. Unwrap and inspect with `errors.Is` (sentinel match) and `errors.As` (type match).

## Sentinels vs types

Export sentinel errors (`var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...)`) for simple checks; custom error types when callers need extra fields.

codeSamples.title: Wrap and check

lessons.title: Packages, visibility, and imports
lessons.body:
## Exported = Capitalized

An identifier is exported (public) if it starts with an uppercase letter; lowercase is package-private. That's the entire access-control system.

## Package design

One directory = one package. Name packages after what they provide (`http`, `json`), not generic names like `utils`.

## init

`init()` runs once at package load — use sparingly (registration, not heavy work).

codeSamples.title: Exported vs private
codeSamples.code:
package money

type Amount struct{ cents int64 } // private field

func New(cents int64) Amount { return Amount{cents} } // exported

lessons.title: Interfaces and implicit satisfaction
lessons.body:
## Structural typing

A type satisfies an interface just by having the methods — no `implements` keyword. This enables loose coupling and easy testing.

## Small interfaces

Go favors tiny interfaces (`io.Reader`, `io.Writer`). Accept interfaces, return concrete types.

## The empty interface / any

`any` (alias for `interface{}`) holds anything. Use type assertions or type switches to recover the concrete type.

codeSamples.title: Type switch

lessons.title: JSON encoding and struct tags
lessons.body:
## Marshal/Unmarshal

`encoding/json` maps structs to JSON. **Exported** fields are (de)serialized; struct tags rename and control them.

## Tags

`json:"name,omitempty"` renames and drops zero values. Use `-` to skip a field.

## Streaming

`json.Decoder`/`Encoder` work over `io.Reader`/`Writer` for HTTP bodies and large payloads.

codeSamples.title: Struct tags

lessons.title: Generics: type parameters and constraints
lessons.body:
## Type parameters

Go 1.18+ supports generics: `func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U`. Constraints restrict allowed types.

## Constraints

`any`, `comparable`, and interfaces with type sets (`constraints.Ordered`). Define your own with unions like `~int | ~float64`.

## When to use

Containers and algorithm helpers benefit. Don't genericize everything — concrete code is often clearer.

codeSamples.title: Generic Map

lessons.title: slices and maps helper packages
lessons.body:
## Batteries included

The generic `slices` and `maps` packages remove hand-rolled loops: `slices.Contains`, `slices.Sort`, `slices.Index`, `maps.Keys`, `maps.Clone`.

## Sorting

`slices.SortFunc` takes a comparison returning -1/0/1; pair with `cmp.Compare`.

## Iterators

Go 1.23+ adds range-over-func iterators; `maps.Keys` now returns an iterator you can range over.

codeSamples.title: Sort with cmp

lessons.title: Goroutines and channels
lessons.body:
## Goroutines

`go f()` starts a lightweight, scheduler-managed coroutine. Cheap to create — but you must control their lifetime.

## Channels

Typed conduits for communication. Unbuffered channels synchronize sender and receiver; buffered channels decouple up to capacity.

## select

`select` waits on multiple channel operations — the backbone of timeouts and cancellation.

Remember: **don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.**

codeSamples.title: select with timeout

lessons.title: sync: Mutex, WaitGroup, Once
lessons.body:
## When channels aren't the answer

For protecting shared in-memory state (caches, counters), a `sync.Mutex` is simpler than channels.

## WaitGroup

Wait for a set of goroutines to finish. `Add` before starting, `Done` in a defer, `Wait` to join.

## Once and RWMutex

`sync.Once` guarantees one-time init. `sync.RWMutex` allows many readers or one writer. The `-race` detector finds data races.

codeSamples.title: WaitGroup

lessons.title: Testing and table-driven tests
lessons.body:
## Built-in testing

Files ending in `_test.go`, functions `TestXxx(t *testing.T)`. Run with `go test ./...`.

## Table-driven

The idiomatic pattern: a slice of cases in a loop, often with `t.Run(name, ...)` subtests for clear failures.

## Coverage and benchmarks

`go test -cover` and `BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` come free. Use `t.Parallel()` where safe.

codeSamples.title: Table-driven test

lessons.title: net/http servers and clients
lessons.body:
## Server

The stdlib is production-grade. Go 1.22+ `http.ServeMux` supports method + path patterns (`GET /users/{id}`) with wildcards.

## Handlers

A handler is `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`. Wrap handlers with middleware for logging/auth.

## Client

Reuse a single `http.Client` with a timeout; always `defer resp.Body.Close()` and drain the body to reuse connections.

codeSamples.title: Routed handler

lessons.title: context for cancellation and deadlines
lessons.body:
## Carry cancellation

`context.Context` propagates deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values through call chains.

## Usage

Take `ctx` as the first parameter. Derive with `context.WithTimeout`/`WithCancel` and always `defer cancel()`.

## Respect it

Check `ctx.Err()` or select on `ctx.Done()` in loops and blocking waits. Don't store context in structs.

codeSamples.title: Timeout context
codeSamples.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()

req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil)
resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)

lessons.title: Modules, versioning, and tooling
lessons.body:
## Dependency management

`go get` adds/updates deps in `go.mod`; `go.sum` locks checksums. `go mod tidy` prunes unused and adds missing.

## Semantic import versioning

Major version v2+ appears in the import path (`.../v2`). Minimal Version Selection picks the lowest version that satisfies all requirements — reproducible builds.

## Vet and vulncheck

`go vet` catches suspicious code; `govulncheck` scans for known CVEs in your dependency graph.

codeSamples.title: Common commands
codeSamples.code:
go get example.com/pkg@v1.4.0
go mod tidy
go vet ./...
govulncheck ./...

lessons.title: Goroutine lifecycles, context, and channels
lessons.body:
## Predictable concurrency

Starting a goroutine is cheap; **owning** its lifetime is the senior skill. Every goroutine needs a purpose, a stop signal, and a way to report failure.

## Context

Pass `context.Context` into anything that waits. Cancel on request abandonment, timeouts, and shutdown. Never store contexts in structs long-term as a rule of thumb — pass them as the first argument.

## Channels vs mutexes

- Channels: ownership transfer, pipelines, signaling.
- Mutexes: protecting shared in-memory state (maps, caches).

Close channels from the **producer**. Prefer `errgroup` for bounded fan-out with cancellation.

codeSamples.title: Bounded work with errgroup

lessons.title: Idiomatic Go: domains over layers
lessons.body:
## Stop writing Java in Go

Deep `service/` / `repository/` / `pkg/` trees often fight Go's package model. Organize by **what the code does** (domain), keep packages small, and prefer the standard library.

## Interfaces

Accept interfaces, return concrete types. Define interfaces where they are **used**, not where they are implemented.

## Testing

Table-driven tests + simple stubs beat heavy mock frameworks for most services.

## Observability

Use `pprof`. Know the new **goroutine leak** profile for stuck blocked goroutines.

codeSamples.title: Table-driven test

lessons.title: Generics, workers, and backpressure
lessons.body:
## Generics

Use `slices` and `maps` helpers. Prefer package-level generic functions when clearer than methods. Go 1.27 adds **generic methods** on concrete types — great for chainable containers; they still cannot satisfy interfaces.

## Worker pools

- `errgroup.SetLimit(n)` for bounded tasks with cancel.
- `semaphore.Weighted` when slots have different weights.
- Bounded channel queues for explicit queue depth.

## Backpressure

Block producers, drop+metric, or reject at the API (HTTP 429). Unbounded queues are how services OOM.

codeSamples.title: slices.SortFunc

lessons.title: Profiling and performance with pprof
lessons.body:
## Measure first

Guessing at performance wastes time. `net/http/pprof` exposes CPU, heap, goroutine, and block profiles at `/debug/pprof/`.

## Workflow

Capture a profile, open it with `go tool pprof`, and inspect `top`, `list`, and flame graphs to find hot paths.

## Allocations

Reduce garbage: reuse buffers with `sync.Pool`, preallocate slices with `make([]T, 0, n)`, and avoid needless pointer indirection. Benchmark with `-benchmem`.
